facts.text: Nuisance braking is an unnecessary automatic brake application; nuisance braking from the decision side occurs when sensors detect something real but the decision logic should have known not to brake.
facts.quote: Nuisance braking is an automatic brake application that was not needed, and "from the decision side" means the cases where the sensors saw something real but the logic should have known not to brake.

facts.text: A false stop can result from decision logic wrongly treating a correctly detected berm, wall, rock pile or spotter as a collision, rather than from a sensor error.
facts.quote: The sensor correctly sees a berm, a wall, a rock pile or a spotter standing where spotters stand; the mistake is deciding that the object is a collision.

facts.text: Tasks that can look like collisions include backing toward a rock pile to load, using a dump berm as a bump stop, dozers and trucks sharing a tip head, working near walls and stockpiles, ground crew and spotters near the machine, tight-clearance parking and workshop maneuvers, and detecting the machine's own tires.
facts.quote: backing toward a rock pile to load, using a dump berm as a bump stop, dozers and trucks sharing a tip head, working close to walls and stockpiles, ground crew and spotters near the machine, parking and workshop maneuvers with small clearances, and the machine detecting its own tires

facts.text: A South African guideline warns that a fixed stop gap can prevent machines from approaching closely enough to be loaded, or force the collision prevention system (CPS) to be switched off.
facts.quote: A South African guideline notes that with a fixed stop gap, machines being loaded "will not be able to come close enough to be loaded or the CPS will have to be switched off" (CPS is a collision prevention system)

facts.text: Decision logic can reduce risk areas using speed, turning angle, barriers and the expected path.
facts.quote: Risk areas can be reduced using speed, turning angle, barriers and the expected path [Chapter 8].

facts.text: Road regulations include false-activation tests requiring driving between two stationary vehicles or over a steel plate without braking.
facts.quote: Road regulations include false-activation tests, such as driving between two stationary vehicles or over a steel plate without braking [Chapters 3, 8].

facts.text: One commercially available wheel-loader system remembers the last slope climbed to prevent activation when reversing down a stockpile, addressing one specific false-activation case.
facts.quote: One wheel-loader system on the market remembers the last slope the machine climbed so that reversing down a stockpile does not trigger it, a targeted fix for one false-activation case [Chapter 2].

facts.text: A collision prevention system cannot suppress the entire loading zone because a second truck or a person can enter that same space.
facts.quote: a system cannot suppress the whole loading zone, because a second truck or a person can enter the same space

facts.text: A collision prevention system should not learn to suppress repeated berm alarms because berm contact is also how fatal dump-edge accidents begin.
facts.quote: it should not "learn away" repeated berm alarms, because berm contact is also how fatal dump-edge accidents begin [Chapter 4].

facts.text: The booklet identifies nuisance interventions as the main documented field failure of deployed proximity systems and the main reason operators switch those systems off.
facts.quote: The booklet calls nuisance interventions "the main documented field failure" of deployed proximity systems and the main reason operators switch them off

facts.text: The nuisance-intervention rate should be an acceptance metric with equal weight to missed interventions.
facts.quote: it says the nuisance-intervention rate should be an acceptance metric equal in weight to missed interventions [Chapter 8].

facts.text: No off-road false-activation rate per operating hour was found.
facts.quote: No off-road false-activation rate per operating hour was found anywhere

facts.text: The program must derive its nuisance-braking acceptance threshold from its own shadow-mode data because no off-road false-activation rate per operating hour was found.
facts.quote: No off-road false-activation rate per operating hour was found anywhere, so the acceptance threshold has to come from the program's own shadow-mode data [Chapters 3, 13].
